_about: Location-specific facts for the /hindi-tutor/<place>/ pages (AdSense plan P3 / D-20, 29 Sep 2026). Applied by tools/apply-tutor-location-specifics.py. 'window' says whether the lesson window printed on the page is standard or summer (daylight-saving) time; 'dst' names the clock-change period or is null; 'tz' is the name of the local clock; 'who' describes who typically learns there; 'script' relates the local writing system to Devanagari; 'start' is the first free guide worth opening from there.

ahmedabad.name: Ahmedabad
ahmedabad.who: Most learners in Ahmedabad already understand Hindi from films and television and want to speak it with confidence at work — Gujarati speakers who switch languages all day, and professionals who have moved in from outside Gujarat.
ahmedabad.script: Gujarati script is close to Devanagari with the top line removed: many letters share their shapes and the vowel signs work the same way, so a Gujarati reader usually reads Hindi within days.
ahmedabad.start: Gujarati readers can skip most of the alphabet and start with greetings, where Hindi and Gujarati politeness differ in small but noticeable ways.

bangalore.name: Bangalore
bangalore.who: Bangalore's learners are mostly people who work with colleagues from north India — Kannada, Tamil, Telugu and Malayalam speakers in tech and services — plus foreign employees posted to the city's offices.
bangalore.script: Kannada script is a Brahmi-family script, like Devanagari: the consonant order (ka, kha, ga, gha, nga) and the way vowel signs attach to consonants are the same, so learning Devanagari is mostly learning new shapes.
bangalore.start: South Indian speakers usually find Hindi's gender agreement the new part, so the grammar-light greetings and numbers guides are a gentle first step.

chandigarh.name: Chandigarh
chandigarh.who: In Chandigarh, Hindi and Punjabi are used side by side; learners here tend to be Punjabi speakers who want formal and written Hindi for exams or government work, and newcomers posted to the city.
chandigarh.script: Gurmukhi, the Punjabi script, belongs to the same Brahmi family as Devanagari and even shares the top line; Punjabi readers recognise the system and several letter shapes.
chandigarh.start: Punjabi speakers already speak much of everyday Hindi, so writing your own name in Devanagari is the quickest way to make the script feel familiar.

chennai.name: Chennai
chennai.who: Chennai is where the Dakshin Bharat Hindi Prachar Sabha was set up in 1918, and its Hindi exams are still taken by many Tamil-speaking students; other learners want Hindi for jobs or postings in north India.
chennai.script: Tamil script is Brahmi-family, like Devanagari, but it writes k, kh, g and gh with one letter; Devanagari gives each its own letter, and hearing those four apart is the main new skill.
chennai.start: Tamil speakers get the most from the alphabet guide first, because it sets out the aspirated and voiced consonants that Tamil spelling does not distinguish.

delhi.name: Delhi
delhi.who: Hindi is Delhi's everyday language, so the learners here are mostly people who arrived from elsewhere — diplomats and expatriates, students from the north-east and the south, and spouses joining Delhi families.
delhi.script: Delhi's shop signs, metro maps and newspapers are in Devanagari, so the script pays off immediately here; learners who read a Latin alphabet usually start with the signs they see every day.
delhi.start: In Delhi the numbers guide pays off first — auto fares, market prices and metro stops are all spoken in Hindi numbers.

hyderabad.name: Hyderabad
hyderabad.who: Hyderabad speaks Telugu and its own Dakhini Hindi-Urdu (hau for yes, nakko for no); learners are often Telugu speakers in tech who want standard Hindi, and newcomers who pick up Dakhini first and want the standard forms.
hyderabad.script: Telugu script is Brahmi-family, like Devanagari, with the same consonant order and vowel signs; many Hyderabadis also read Urdu's Nastaliq, which writes the same spoken language right to left.
hyderabad.start: Learners who already speak Dakhini can go straight to the alphabet guide, since the spoken language is largely there and the script is what is new.

jaipur.name: Jaipur
jaipur.who: Jaipur speaks Hindi alongside Dhundhari and other Rajasthani varieties; learners here include foreigners staying for months in the old city, people working in tourism and crafts, and students from outside the state.
jaipur.script: Rajasthani is written in Devanagari too, so the script on Jaipur's signs, bazaars and bus stands is the one you learn for Hindi.
jaipur.start: In Jaipur the travel phrases guide is the practical first step — bargaining in the bazaars and getting around by auto use exactly those phrases.

kolkata.name: Kolkata
kolkata.who: Kolkata's learners are mostly Bengali speakers who understand Hindi but want to speak it naturally, together with professionals moving to the city who deal with its large Hindi-speaking business communities.
kolkata.script: Bengali script is a sister of Devanagari — the same consonant order, vowel signs and a top line — so reading usually comes quickly; the bigger change is that Hindi verbs and adjectives change for gender and Bengali's do not.
kolkata.start: Bengali speakers usually get the most from the greetings guide, which covers the aap/tum/tu choice Bengali handles differently.

lucknow.name: Lucknow
lucknow.who: Lucknow is known for its polished Hindi-Urdu and its courtesy of address (pehle aap — after you); learners here often want that register, and Urdu readers want to add Devanagari.
lucknow.script: Many Lucknow families read Urdu in Nastaliq; Devanagari writes the same spoken language left to right with every vowel marked, so for them the script is the only new part.
lucknow.start: The greetings guide is the natural first step in Lucknow, because the choice between aap, tum and tu matters more here than almost anywhere.

mumbai.name: Mumbai
mumbai.who: Mumbai runs on Marathi, Gujarati and the city's own Bambaiya Hindi; learners are often expatriates who want standard Hindi rather than street Hindi, and Marathi or Gujarati speakers who want to polish theirs.
mumbai.script: Marathi is written in Devanagari, so Mumbai's signs already use the script; Marathi readers only need to learn a few Hindi spelling habits.
mumbai.start: Newcomers in Mumbai get the most from the fifty travel phrases, which cover trains, autos and food the way the city actually uses them.

patna.name: Patna
patna.who: Around Patna, many people grow up speaking Magahi, Bhojpuri or Maithili and use Hindi at school and work; learners here often want a standard, interview-ready Hindi.
patna.script: Hindi, Magahi, Bhojpuri and Maithili are all written in Devanagari today, so the script is already familiar; the work is in standard spelling and verb forms.
patna.start: For Patna learners who already speak a related language, the numbers guide is a quick check of forms that differ between Hindi and the home language.

pune.name: Pune
pune.who: Pune's learners include Marathi speakers who want fluent Hindi for work and the many students and IT professionals from across India and abroad who live in the city.
pune.script: Marathi is written in Devanagari, so locals already read Hindi's script; newcomers learn the same letters that are on every Pune street sign.
pune.start: Marathi speakers can go straight to greetings and conversation, since the script and much of the vocabulary are already there.

australia.name: Australia
australia.dst: from the first Sunday of October to the first Sunday of April in New South Wales, Victoria, the ACT, Tasmania and South Australia
australia.zones: Australia has three standard zones — AEST (UTC+10) in the east, ACST (UTC+9:30) in South Australia and the Northern Territory, and AWST (UTC+8) in Western Australia — and Queensland, the Northern Territory and Western Australia do not change their clocks, so a Perth learner's window is three hours earlier than Sydney's in summer.
australia.who: Hindi is one of the most widely spoken languages in Australian homes, and learners here are often second-generation Australians or partners of Hindi-speaking families.
australia.script: Australian learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, so once its letters are learned every word can be read exactly as written.
australia.start: Heritage learners who understand Hindi but cannot write it usually start by writing their own name in Devanagari.

canada.name: Canada
canada.dst: from the second Sunday of March to the first Sunday of November (most provinces)
canada.zones: Canada spans six zones; the window here is Eastern Time, so subtract three hours in British Columbia and add one and a half in Newfoundland.
canada.who: Canada's learners are often children and grandchildren of Indian immigrants, or partners in Punjabi- and Hindi-speaking families in Ontario and British Columbia.
canada.script: Canadian learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, so once its letters are learned words are read exactly as written — unlike English or French spelling.
canada.start: Canadian heritage learners usually begin with greetings, which teach the respectful forms used with elders.

dubai.name: Dubai
dubai.who: In Dubai, Hindi is a working language across construction, retail and hospitality, so learners are often managers, business owners and long-term residents who want to speak directly with staff and customers.
dubai.script: Arabic readers switch direction for Devanagari — left to right instead of right to left — and find every vowel written, which makes sounding words out easier than in Arabic.
dubai.start: In Dubai the numbers guide pays off first, because prices, quantities and phone numbers are where misunderstandings cost money.

germany.name: Germany
germany.dst: from the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October (CEST, UTC+2)
germany.who: Germany has a long academic tradition of studying Sanskrit and Indian languages, and today's learners are often partners of Indian professionals, students, and people preparing for travel or work in India.
germany.script: German readers use a Latin alphabet with fairly regular spelling; Devanagari is more regular still, with one symbol for each sound.
germany.start: German speakers already have the ch sound of Bach, close to Hindi's kh in khana; the alphabet guide shows which Hindi sounds German lacks.

houston.name: Houston
houston.dst: from the second Sunday of March to the first Sunday of November
houston.who: Houston has one of the largest Indian communities in the United States, with its own Mahatma Gandhi District along Hillcroft Avenue; learners are often heritage speakers and partners in Indian families.
houston.script: Texan learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, so once its letters are learned words are read exactly as written.
houston.start: Houston learners who can already follow family conversations often start with greetings and polite forms, the part most heritage speakers were never taught.

japan.name: Japan
japan.who: Japanese learners of Hindi are often students of Indian culture and Buddhism, business people working with Indian partners, and fans of Indian films.
japan.script: The order of the Japanese kana table (a, i, u, e, o; ka, sa, ta, na, ha, ma) was modelled on the sound order of Sanskrit, the same order Devanagari follows, so the alphabet chart will look strangely logical.
japan.start: Japanese speakers already have pure vowels close to Hindi's; the alphabet guide shows the aspirated and retroflex sounds Japanese lacks.

london.name: London
london.dst: from the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October (BST, UTC+1)
london.who: London's learners are often second-generation British Indians who understand family conversations but cannot join them, plus partners and colleagues of Hindi speakers.
london.script: London learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, so once its letters are learned every word is read exactly as written.
london.start: Heritage learners in London often start by writing their own name in Hindi, then move to greetings to practise the respectful forms.

melbourne.name: Melbourne
melbourne.dst: from the first Sunday of October to the first Sunday of April (AEDT, UTC+11)
melbourne.who: Melbourne's Indian community has grown quickly with students and skilled migrants, and many learners are partners, children or colleagues of Hindi speakers.
melbourne.script: Melbourne learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, so once its letters are learned words are read exactly as written.
melbourne.start: Melbourne learners who want to speak with family usually begin with greetings and the numbers guide.

nepal.name: Nepal
nepal.who: Most Nepalis understand spoken Hindi from films and television; learners here usually want to speak it accurately for work, study or travel in India.
nepal.script: Nepali is written in Devanagari, so there is nothing new to learn: every letter and vowel sign in Hindi is one you already read.
nepal.start: Nepali speakers can skip the alphabet entirely and go straight to the greetings guide, which shows where Hindi and Nepali polite forms differ.

new-york.name: New York
new-york.dst: from the second Sunday of March to the first Sunday of November
new-york.who: New York's learners include heritage speakers from Queens and New Jersey's Indian neighbourhoods, partners in Indian families, and professionals working with Indian teams.
new-york.script: New York learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, so once its letters are learned words are read exactly as written.
new-york.start: New Yorkers working with teams in India often start with the numbers guide, then greetings for meetings and calls.

san-francisco.name: the San Francisco Bay Area
san-francisco.dst: from the second Sunday of March to the first Sunday of November
san-francisco.who: Bay Area learners are often engineers who work with colleagues in India, their partners, and children of Indian families in Fremont, Sunnyvale and San Jose.
san-francisco.script: Bay Area learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, so once its letters are learned words are read exactly as written.
san-francisco.start: Engineers who work with colleagues in India often start with greetings and the numbers guide, which cover most small talk on a call.

singapore.name: Singapore
singapore.who: Hindi is one of the Indian languages offered in Singapore's schools, so many learners are students and parents, alongside professionals working with India.
singapore.script: Tamil readers in Singapore already know a Brahmi-family script with the same consonant order and vowel signs; English and Chinese readers meet a fully phonetic system.
singapore.start: Students in Singapore usually start with the alphabet guide and its printable chart.

south-africa.name: South Africa
south-africa.who: South Africa's Indian community goes back to 1860, and Hindi is often a heritage language that families want to keep — many learners are adults reconnecting with it.
south-africa.script: South African learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, so once its letters are learned words are read exactly as written.
south-africa.start: Heritage learners in South Africa often start with greetings and family words, the vocabulary most often lost across generations.

spain.name: Spain
spain.dst: from the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October (CEST, UTC+2)
spain.zones: The Canary Islands keep a clock one hour behind the mainland, so their window starts an hour earlier.
spain.who: Spain's learners are often travellers planning longer stays in India, students of yoga and Indian culture, and partners of Indian professionals.
spain.script: Spanish spelling is regular and so is Devanagari: once the letters are learned, words are read exactly as written.
spain.start: Spanish speakers already have pure vowels and a tapped r; the alphabet guide shows the aspirated and retroflex sounds Spanish lacks.

sydney.name: Sydney
sydney.dst: from the first Sunday of October to the first Sunday of April (AEDT, UTC+11)
sydney.who: Sydney's Indian community centres on suburbs such as Harris Park, and learners are often second-generation Australians and partners in Hindi-speaking families.
sydney.script: Sydney learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, so once its letters are learned words are read exactly as written.
sydney.start: Sydney learners often begin with greetings and the fifty travel phrases before a family trip to India.

toronto.name: Toronto
toronto.dst: from the second Sunday of March to the first Sunday of November
toronto.who: Greater Toronto, including Brampton and Mississauga, is home to one of the largest South Asian communities in North America, and learners are often heritage speakers and partners of Hindi speakers.
toronto.script: Toronto learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, so once its letters are learned words are read exactly as written.
toronto.start: Toronto heritage learners often start by writing their own name in Hindi, then move to greetings.

united-arab-emirates.name: the UAE
united-arab-emirates.who: Indians are the largest community in the UAE, so learners across the Emirates are often employers, managers and residents who want to talk directly with colleagues and staff.
united-arab-emirates.script: Arabic readers switch direction for Devanagari — left to right — and find every vowel written, which makes reading aloud predictable.
united-arab-emirates.start: In the UAE the fifty travel phrases and the numbers guide cover most everyday workplace exchanges.

united-kingdom.name: the United Kingdom
united-kingdom.dst: from the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October (BST, UTC+1)
united-kingdom.who: Across the UK — Leicester, Birmingham and London above all — learners are often British Indians reconnecting with a family language, and partners of Hindi speakers.
united-kingdom.script: UK learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, so once its letters are learned words are read exactly as written.
united-kingdom.start: UK heritage learners often begin with greetings and family words, then write their own name in Devanagari.

united-states.name: the United States
united-states.dst: from the second Sunday of March to the first Sunday of November (not in Hawaii or most of Arizona)
united-states.zones: The window here is Eastern Time; subtract one hour for Central, two for Mountain and three for Pacific time.
united-states.who: The United States has the largest Indian diaspora in the world, so learners range from heritage speakers and their children to partners, colleagues and students.
united-states.script: American learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, so once its letters are learned words are read exactly as written.
united-states.start: Heritage learners in the US often start with greetings, the respectful forms used with elders.

worldwide.name: anywhere in the world
worldwide.who: This page is for learners outside the cities and countries listed elsewhere; the tutors teach online, so where you live only changes the hours.
worldwide.script: Whatever alphabet you read now, Devanagari is phonetic: once its letters are learned, words are read exactly as written.
worldwide.start: Wherever you are, the alphabet guide and its printable chart are the best first step if you want to read.
